records.targetRef: Tiferet Yosef, Ha'azinu and Shabbat Shuvah 6
records.themeTitle: Guidance while the final result is still concealed
records.themeSummary: The verse about a word from behind can also describe Torah holding a person to the path during concealment.
records.explanation: Rav Tzadok emphasizes the end at which an action becomes known; Tiferet Yosef reads the same ‘word from behind you’ as Torah holding a person to Hashem's will while clarity is absent. The readings are complementary rather than identical. The second explains how to continue the effort and hope required by the siman without pretending to know the final verdict.
records.targetEnglish: ‘May my teaching drop like rain; may my utterance flow like dew.’ My holy grandfather explained ya'arof as related to the back of the neck: some words of Torah hold a person from behind his neck and do not let him turn from Hashem's will. If a person clearly recognized direct light from Hashem and stood face to face before Him, there would be no place for service; he would recognize explicitly that departing from His will by a hair's breadth is departing from life. Because Hashem desires to benefit His creatures, He concealed this light, and a person does not stand so directly face to face. He must break through the concealment, recognize Hashem's light explicitly, and stand face to face again. Thus, when receiving prophecy, the prophet said, ‘Thus says Hashem,’ standing face to face and recognizing His will explicitly. The Talmud says (Megillah 32a): from where is it known that one may make use of a heavenly echo? From ‘Your ears will hear a word from behind you’ (Isaiah 30:21). When the person is in concealment, he must recognize Hashem's light from behind: he must attend to the words of Torah that hold him within the concealment so he does not turn from His will. This is called a heavenly echo. Those words of Torah that hold him within concealment are called ‘May my teaching drop like rain.’ When he breaks through the concealment and stands face to face before Hashem's light, this signifies ‘May my utterance flow like dew.’

records.targetRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Miketz 6
records.themeTitle: Interpreting the world through the life within it
records.themeSummary: A world likened to a dream is clarified by recognizing the divine utterance that sustains it.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach develops the siman's dream analogy through an ordinary act: eating bread. Receiving only the outward food gives temporal life, while recognizing Hashem's utterance within it connects the act to enduring life. This helps explain why Rav Tzadok locates the power of interpretation in Torah and in the person's attachment to truth, rather than in an arbitrary favorable statement about events.
records.targetEnglish: ‘You hear a dream to interpret it.’ All the matters of this world are like a dream requiring interpretation, and as a person interprets it, so it is established with him. The person who understands in everything that all is only from Hashem and that all lives through the utterance of His mouth understands the meaning in every matter and reaches true life. With bread, for example, the principal life-giving element within it is the utterance of Hashem's mouth. Someone who eats simply like an animal receives from the bread only the life of this world. Someone who understands that Hashem's utterance gives life attains enduring life. For the letters of lechem, bread, are those of chalom, dream: it requires interpretation. So it is with all pleasures, for all the pleasures and benefits in the world are likened to bread.
records.originHebrew: וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שָׁם נה:): הַחֲלוֹמוֹת הוֹלְכִים אַחַר הַפֶּה הַיְינוּ בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה יָכוֹל לְבָרֵר כָּל מַעֲשִׂים שֶׁעָשָׂה יִהְיֶה לְטוֹב, וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהָיוּ אֵיךְ שֶׁהָיוּ, עַל יְדֵי הַפֶּה הוּא נַעֲשֶׂה טוֹב, שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵאִיר עֵינָיו בָּזֶה, וְאָז נִקְבָּע הַחֲלוֹם לֶאֱמֶת כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל, דְּתוֹרָה הִיא אֱמֶת;
records.originEnglish: And regarding this our Sages stated (ibid. 55b): dreams follow the mouth— meaning through words of Torah, for through words of Torah one can clarify all deeds he has done so that they result in good; and even though they were as they were, through the mouth they become good, as the Blessed Name enlightens his eyes in this, and then the dream is established as truth as noted above, for Torah is Truth;
records.targetHebrew: תִּשְׁמַע חֲלוֹם לִפְתֹּר אוֹתוֹ. הַיְינוּ כִּי כָּל עִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה הֵם כַּחֲלוֹם הַצָּרִיךְ פִּתְרוֹן וּכְמוֹ שֶׁיִּפְתּוֹר לוֹ הָאָדָם כֵּן יָקוּם אֶצְלוֹ, וְהָאָדָם הַמֵּבִין בַּכֹּל כִּי הַכֹּל הוּא רַק מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְרַק מִמּוֹצָא פִיו יִחְיֶה הַכֹּל, זֶה מֵבִין טַעַם בְּכָל דָּבָר וּמַגִּיעַ לְחַיִּים אֲמִיתִּיִּים, כְּמוֹ לֶחֶם הָעִיקָּר הַמְחַיֶּה הַנִּמְצָא בּוֹ הוּא הַמּוֹצָא פִּי הַשֵּׁם וּמִי שֶׁאוֹכֵל פָּשׁוּט כִּבְהֵמָה, אֵינוֹ מַשִּׂיג מֵהַלֶּחֶם רַק חַיֵּי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה, וְהַמֵּבִין כִּי מוֹצָא פִּי הַשֵּׁם הוּא הַמְחַיֶּה זֶה יַשִּׂיג חַיֵּי עוֹלָם, כִּי לֶחֶם הוּא אוֹתִיּוֹת חֲלֹם הַיְינוּ שֶׁצָּרִיךְ פִּתְרוֹן, וְכֵן הוּא כָּל הֲנָאוֹת, כִּי כָּל הַהֲנָאוֹת וְהַטּוֹבוֹת שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם נִמְשָׁלִין לְלֶחֶם.

records.targetRef: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua 10
records.themeTitle: The leader and the generation’s combined soul
records.themeSummary: A generation’s many spiritual powers are described as gathered in its leader.
records.explanation: Likkutei Maamarim explains the siman's statement that the generation's thoughts and desires build the stature of its leader. Their gathering is itself described as a distinct soul, with the leader including their wisdom and powers. This makes the relation reciprocal rather than a claim about popularity, and clarifies why the siman discusses the generation's brief illumination and its leader together.
records.targetEnglish: It is known that the leader of a generation has a soul encompassing all the souls of that generation, as the Sages said (Arakhin 17a), a leader according to the generation, and a generation according to the leader. Every generation is a particular arrangement of the souls of that generation—that is, parts of Hashem's wisdom, as explained. The gathering of all those wisdoms is itself also one soul. Souls divide into details and further details according to the order Hashem arranged, and their totality is itself a distinct soul, different from the details taken alone. The father's soul includes the souls of all his children; Adam included the souls of all the generations, and their totality was Adam's distinct soul. Likewise, the leader's soul includes all the generation's souls, as a king is the whole nation. He can therefore lead them all, because his wisdom includes all their wisdom, and likewise his understanding and all his spiritual powers.
records.originHebrew: פֵּירוּשׁ, כִּי מִמַּחֲשָׁבוֹת וּרְצוֹנוֹת הַטּוֹבוֹת שֶׁבְּיִשְׂרָאֵל נִבְנֶה קוֹמַת הַנָּבִיא וַחֲכַם הַדּוֹר, וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ (עֲרָכִין יז.): פַּרְנָס לְפִי הַדּוֹר; וְאָמְרוּ: אֵיזֶה דוֹר חָבִיב וְכוּלֵי? דּוֹר הַמִּדְבָּר, וְהָיָה אָז פַּרְנָס מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "לֹא קָם וְגוֹמֵר".
records.originEnglish: meaning that from the good thoughts and aspirations of Israel the stature of the prophet and the sage of the generation is constructed, and therefore they said (Arachin 17a): a leader is according to the generation; and they said: which generation is most beloved? The Generation of the Wilderness, whose leader was Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, of whom it is said: "and there arose not a prophet since in Israel like unto Moses" (Deuteronomy 34:10).
records.targetHebrew: כי דבר ידוע שפרנס הדור נפשו כוללת כל נפשות הדור, כמה שאמרו זכרונם לברכה בערכין (י״ז עמוד א׳): פרנס לפי הדור, וכן דור לפי הפרנס; והיינו שכל דור הוא סדר מיחד מנפשות מאותו הדור, שרצונו לומר חלקי חכמות של השם יתברך כנזכר, וקבוץ כל החכמות כלם ביחד, קבוצם הוא גם כן נפש אחת, כמו שהוא בעניני הנפשות שמתחלקים לפרטים ופרטי פרטות עד כפי סדר החלקה שסדר השם יתברך, וכללותם הוא גם כן נפש פרטית בפני עצמה משנה מהפרטים לבדם, וכמו שכל נפש האב כלול בו נפשות כל בניו, וכן באדם הראשון כלול נפשות כל הדורות, וכללותם הוא נפש פרטית של אדם הראשון; וכן בכל הדור, נפש פרנס ומנהיג הדור היא נפש הכוללת כל נפשות הדור, כמו שהמלך הוא כלל כל האמה, ולכך יוכל להנהיגם כלם, כי חכמתו כוללת חכמת כלם, וכן דעתו וכל כחותיו הנפשיים;

records.themeTitle: Faith that does not force the time
records.themeSummary: Hope in a spiritual rescue can be patient while the path remains hidden.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains the same ‘trust in Hashem’ passage through a definition of faith: holding to what has not yet become clear without forcing its time. This qualifies the siman's permission to hope for an unexpected spiritual rescue. The hope accompanies its stated first response of doing good and prayer; it is not a timetable imposed on the rescue.
records.targetEnglish: Emunah is related to ‘as a nurse carries the infant.’ As the Tikkunei Zohar explains (introduction, 2a), ‘the father of faith, which is understanding.’ One should not hasten the time or press the hour, but wait in faith. Then this kindness will be revealed, and he will recognize it within his understanding too. ‘Tend faith’ means to guard the matter until it is also revealed in one's understanding. The term faith applies only to what is not explicit in one's understanding: what is already explicit needs no faith. What is not explicit requires faith—guarding the matter well until it emerges into explicit revelation before human eyes.
records.originHebrew: וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: "בְּטַח בַּה' וַעֲשֵׂה טוֹב וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים לז, ג), וְלֹא יָחוּשׁ שֶׁחַס וְשָׁלוֹם הַמַּעֲשִׂים טוֹבִים לָרִיק; וְכֵן אִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר (תּוֹלְדוֹת קמב עַמּוּד א) עַל פָּסוּק "עָז לוֹ בָךְ" (שָׁם פד, ו) – הַיְינוּ לְעִנְיָן זֶה, שֶׁ"מְסִלּוֹת בִּלְבָבָם", שֶׁיַּעַזְרֶנּוּ וִיהַפֵּךְ לִבּוֹ לְטוֹב, עַל זֶה יוּכַל לִסְמוֹךְ וְלֹא כַּחֲמוֹר וְכוּלֵי, עַיֵּין שָׁם. וּ"מְסִלּוֹת" רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר שֶׁאֵינוֹ הַדֶּרֶךְ כְּבוּשָׁה, רַק הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ יָכוֹל לַעֲשׂוֹת מְסִלָּה מִן הַצַּד בִּלְבָבָם לְטוֹבָה.
records.originEnglish: and concerning this it is stated: "Trust in Hashem, and do good, etc." (Psalms 37:3), and let him not worry that his good deeds are in vain, Heaven forbid; and so it is stated in the Zohar (Toldot 142a) on the verse "whose strength is in You" (Psalms 84:6)—meaning in this regard, that "highways are in their heart," that He will assist him and overturn his heart to good; on this he may rely, and not be like a stubborn donkey, etc., see there. And "highways" (mesilot) denotes that it is not the paved public road, but the Blessed Name can forge a highway from the side within their hearts for the good.
records.targetHebrew: ואמונה הוא מלשון כאשר ישא האומן את היונק והוא כמבואר בתזוה"ק (הקדמה דף ב.) אב האמונה דאיהו בינה וכו' היינו שלא יחפוז את הזמן ולא תדחק את השעה רק שימתין את הזמן באמונתו. אזי יתגלה זה החסד ויכיר אותו גם בהבנת תפיסתו. וזהו ורעה אמונה כלומר להיות שמר את הדבר עד שיתגלה גם בהתפיסה. כי הלשון אמונה אינו נופל כי אם על דבר שאינו מפורש בהתפיסה. כי בזה שהוא מפורש בהתפיסה. אין מהצורך להאמונה. רק בזאת שאינו מפורש בהתפיסה צריכין אמונה היינו שיהיה שמר היטב את הדבר עד שיצא בהתגלות מפורש גם לעיני אדם.

records.themeTitle: Prayer that reawakens Torah acquired through effort
records.themeSummary: The loss of felt illumination need not erase what labor has established in the heart.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef adds a distinction to the siman's account of first light and prayer. A gift can be lost when attention moves away; Torah acquired through effort becomes fixed enough to be awakened again through prayer. This explains a way in which the plea to preserve the first desire works together with the learner's subsequent labor.
records.targetEnglish: When Hashem gives a person illumination of understanding in the light of Torah, without the person having endured or labored for those words of Torah, then if he turns his attention away even for a moment, Scripture says (Proverbs 23:5), ‘Will you set your eyes upon it? It is gone.’ As the Jerusalem Talmud says at the end of Berakhot in the name of the Scroll of the Pious: if you leave it one day, it leaves you two. But Torah that comes through labor, for which the person has endured, becomes fixed in his heart and will not let him turn away. As it says (Deuteronomy 32:2), ‘May my teaching drop like rain’: my holy grandfather explained that Torah for which a person labors holds him from behind his neck and will not let him turn away, like someone holding his fellow so he cannot leave. If the person nevertheless turns away from Torah that came through labor, he can reawaken it through much prayer and regain his former illumination. Through the endurance and labor he devoted to it, it became fixed in his heart, and he can reawaken the Torah repeatedly through prayer.
records.originHebrew: וְהָעֵצָה לָזֶה – תְּפִלָּה, כִּידוּעַ דְּהַתְחָלָה הוּא מַדְרֵגַת אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם וְהוּא "פֵּתַח דְּבָרֶיךָ", וְהַסּוֹף שֶׁחוֹזֵר לְהָאִיר הוּא דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם וּמָשִׁיחַ, וְהוּא דַּרְגָּא דִּתְפִלָּה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וַאֲנִי תְפִלָּה" (שָׁם קט, ד).
records.originEnglish: And the spiritual remedy for this is prayer, for as is known, the beginning is the attribute of our father Abraham, peace be upon him, which is "the opening of Your words," and the culmination when the light returns to shine is King David, peace be upon him, and the Messiah, which is the spiritual rung of prayer, as written: "and I am prayer" (Psalms 109:4).
records.targetHebrew: כשהשי"ת נותן להאדם הארת הדעת באור דברי תורה, ולא היה להאדם שום סבלנות ויגיעה על הד"ת האלו, אז אם הוא מסיח דעת מזה רגע אחת, על זה נאמר (משלי כ״ג:ה׳) התעיף עיניך בו ואיננו. וכמו שאיתא בירושלמי (סוף ברכות בשם מגילת חסידים) אם תעזבנו יום יומים יעזביך. אמנם הד"ת שבא לאדם ביגיעה והיה לו סבלנות על זה הד"ת, אלו נקבעים בלבו בקביעות שלא יניח לו להסיח דעת מהם, כמו שכתיב (דברים ל״ב:ב׳) יערוף כמטר לקחי וגו', וביאר בזה כבוד אזמו"ר הגה"ק זללה"ה, היינו הד"ת שאדם מיגע עליה, היא אוחזת את האדם מאחורי עורפו ואינה מניחה לו שיסיח דעת ממנה, כמו שהאדם אוחז בחבירו ואינו מניח לו לילך ממנו. ובאם יזדמן שהאדם יסיח דעת מהד"ת שבא לו ביגיעה, אז בכחו לעורר את הד"ת בחזרה כשירבה בתפלה על זה, ויהיה לו אותו הארת הדעת כמקודם, מפני שעל ידי סבלנות ויגיעה שהיה לו עליה נקבע בלבו בקביעות, ויכול פעם בפעם לעורר הד"ת על ידי תפלה.

records.themeTitle: The thought that holds the heart’s life
records.themeSummary: A central attachment is distinguished from the outer passing garments of thought.
records.explanation: Machshavot Charutz makes an explicit distinction relevant to ‘where his thought is attached.’ The thought carrying the heart's central life defines the person at depth; other thoughts can be outer garments. It also acknowledges how difficult it is to be entirely free of a momentary other thought. This helps read the siman's language of attachment with precision while preserving the task of directing thought toward Torah.
records.targetEnglish: A thought of this kind, upon which the heart's principal point of life depends, is the essence of the person—not the other outer thoughts, which are garments of the inward and principal thought. Almost no person is completely pure even in thought's outer garment, belonging to Hashem alone so that no other thought rises in his mind for even one moment throughout his life.
records.originHebrew: וּמָקוֹם שֶׁמַּחֲשַׁבְתּוֹ אֲדוּקָה, כָּךְ הוּא כָּל צוּרַת הָאָדָם בְּאוֹתוֹ עֵת.
records.originEnglish: And where his thought is bound fast, such is the entire form of the person at that moment.
records.targetHebrew: ומחשבה כזו שעקר נקדת החיות שבלב נתלה בה זהו עקר האדם לא שאר מחשבות חיצוניות שהם לבושי המחשבה הפנימיית והעקריית, וכמעט אין אדם שיהיה נקי לגמרי גם בלבוש החיצוני מהמחשבה שיהיה בלתי לה' לבדו ולא יעלה כל ימיו על מחשבתו רגע אחד הרהור אחר

records.themeTitle: The mitzvah itself as the future delight
records.themeSummary: The good tasted after labor is described as a deeper enjoyment of the service itself.
records.explanation: Peri Tzadik explains the continuity between a person's embodied service and the good tasted afterward. Torah and the mitzvah meal become the very forms of future delight, rather than a reward detached from the service. This develops the siman's final distinction between the deed alone and enjoyment that makes its inward life perceptible.
records.targetEnglish: It is known that the reward of a mitzvah is the mitzvah itself: one merits that very matter. Thus Torah scholars have no rest in the world to come, as it says, ‘They go from strength to strength’ (Berakhot 64a). Through their engagement in Torah in this world, they merit delighting in Torah in the world to come. Likewise, through the mitzvah meal they observe in this world, they merit the feast of the righteous in the future, which is the culmination of holy delight, as explained in the holy books. As the Sages said: through fulfilling the mitzvah of sukkah one merits sitting in the sukkah of Leviathan's skin.
records.originHebrew: וְהוּא בָּא אַחֲרֵי הַיְגִיעַ כַּפַּיִם בְּמַעֲשֶׂה, אַחַר כָּךְ מְהַנִּים אוֹתוֹ מִלְּמַעְלָה מֵעֵין עוֹלָם הַבָּא, וְאָז זוֹכֶה לְ"טוֹב לָךְ" גַּם בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא:   (אות קמו) (מכתב יד קדשו).
records.originEnglish: which follows after physical toil in practical deed, whereupon they bestow pleasure upon him from Above as a foretaste of the World to Come, and then he merits "and it shall be good with you" in the World to Come as well.  This entire section was censored and omitted from the first printed edition of Tzidkas HaTzaddik. It was subsequently restored from a transcript made by one of the close disciples of the author, Rav Tzadok HaKohen of Lublin, who copied it directly from his holy handwritten manuscript (from his holy handwritten manuscript).
records.targetHebrew: כי ידוע ששכר מצוה הוא המצוה בעצמה היינו שיזכה בזה הענין בעצמו. כעניון ת"ח אין להם מנוחה בעוה"ב שנא' ילכו מחיל אל חיל (ברכות ס"ד.) והיינו שע"י עסקם בתורה בעוה"ז יזכו לעוה"ב להתענג בעסק ד"ת וכמו"כ ע"י הסעודת מצוה שמקיימים בהעוה"ז יזכו עי"ז להסעודה של הצדיקים לע"ל שהוא תכלית העונג של הקדושה כידוע בסה"ק וכאמרם ז"ל שע"י קיום מצות סוכה יזכה לישב בסוכת עורו של לויתן:

records.themeTitle: The garment’s appearance and the soul’s root
records.themeSummary: A pleasing outward form and an inward spiritual quality are distinct matters.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim develops the same verse about servants on horses and princes walking on the ground. Its contrast concerns the relation between outward garment and root: an attractive appearance can conceal a deficiency, while a coarse appearance can conceal a root without that deficiency. This explains the siman's distinction without making bodily appearance alone a reliable measure of a person's inward quality.
records.targetEnglish: Ashur and Egypt are alluded to in ‘I have seen servants on horses, and princes walking like servants on the earth’ (Ecclesiastes 10:7). My holy father explained: servants on horses indicate very beautiful and clean garments, while there is a deficiency at the root. As the Tikkunei Zohar says (Tikkun 60), evil within and a beautiful garment outside—of this it says, ‘I have seen servants on horses.’ Princes walking like servants on the earth indicate coarse and darkened garments, while at their root there is no deficiency.
records.originHebrew: דְּיֵשׁ נְפָשׁוֹת גְּדוֹלוֹת בְּגוּפִים מְכֹעָרִים, וְכֵן לְהֵיפֶךְ. וְהוּא סוֹד תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה וְשֶׁבִּכְתָב,
records.originEnglish: that there are great souls within plain/unattractive bodies, and likewise the reverse. And this is the mystical secret of the Oral Torah and the Written Torah,
records.targetHebrew: אמנם הענין הוא כי אשור ומצרים רומזים כדכתיב (קהלת י׳:ז׳) ראיתי עבדים על סוסים ושרים הולכים כעבדים על הארץ. וביאר בזה אאמו"ר הגה"ק זצללחה"ה עבדים על סוסים מורה על לבושים יפים ונקיים מאד ובהשרש יש להם חסרון וכמבואר בתקוני זוה"ק (תקון שתין) רע מלגאו ולבושא דיליה שפיר מלבר על האי אתמר ראיתי עבדים על סוסים, ושרים הולכים על הארץ כעבדים מורה על לבושים גסים ועכורים אבל בשורשם אין בהם שום חסרון

records.themeTitle: Purity within the same garment
records.themeSummary: The higher unity can reveal purity where the outward form had seemed to show its opposite.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains the same question, ‘Who can bring pure from impure—is it not One?’ Its point is the disclosure of purity within the very garment that previously seemed impure, rather than merely replacing that garment. This develops why Rav Tzadok links the paradox to divine unity and why Bilaam's view of the outward act alone misses the source of its holiness.
records.targetEnglish: It is written (Job 14:4), ‘Who can bring pure from impure—is it not One?’ This means being able to see purity in the very form of the garment that previously appeared to show its opposite, without the garment itself changing. This is possible only when illumination shines from the highest place, called One, indicating One beyond reckoning: illumination from the higher will that is removed from all garments and free of all forms.
records.originHebrew: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ עַל זֶה (נִדָּה ט.): "מִי יִתֵּן טָהוֹר מִטָּמֵא? לֹא אֶחָד" (אִיּוֹב יד, ד) – יְחִידוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם;
records.originEnglish: And as our Sages expounded on this (Niddah 9a): "'Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? Not one' (Job 14:4)—the Unique One of the world";
records.targetHebrew: כתיב מי יתן טהור מטמא לא אחד (איוב י״ד:ד׳) היינו שיהי' יכולין לראות טהרה באותו גוון הלבוש בעצמו שמקודם הי' נראה ההיפך והלבוש בעצמו לא ישתנה זה אין יתכן רק כאשר זורח ממקום העליון ביותר הנקרא אחד שמורה על חד ולא בחושבן היינו שיהי' מאיר מזה הרצון עליון שהוא נעתק מכל לבושים ומשולל מכל גוונים

records.themeTitle: The given soul becomes one’s own world
records.themeSummary: The initial gift is attributed to the person through the work by which it is acquired.
records.explanation: Resisei Layla explains the transition from receiving a soul to calling its completed world one's own. The initial gift comes from Hashem; through Torah and mitzvot it becomes attributed to the person who has worked for it. This clarifies the siman's contrast between an insight that is only seen and a perfection that has become a settled acquisition.
records.targetEnglish: Just as Torah is initially ‘Hashem's Torah’ and afterward the person's Torah, so the soul begins with ‘He breathed into his nostrils,’ from Hashem, as we say, ‘The soul You gave me.’ At the end it is called the house of his own world, belonging to him: the soul is called by his name because through his effort he merited it. Thus the Sages said (Vayikra Rabbah 35), ‘As though you made yourselves,’ concerning ‘You shall perform them’ (Leviticus 26:3): through performing Torah and mitzvot one merits this.
records.originHebrew: וְצָרִיךְ הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת עַד שֶׁמַּגִּיעַ לִהְיוֹת כָּךְ בְּקִנְיָן וְנִבְלָע בַּלֵּב כָּל מַה שֶּׁמַּשִּׂיג, וְאָז נִקְרָא "קוֹנֶה עוֹלָמוֹ".
records.originEnglish: and one requires long exertion until he reaches the state where it becomes an internalized acquisition and all that he perceives is absorbed into his heart, and then he is termed "one who acquires his world."
records.targetHebrew: וכמו התורה בתחלה "תורת ה'" וכולי, כך הנפש בתחלה "ויפח וכולי" מהשם יתברך כמו שכתוב: "נשמה שנתת בי", ולבסוף נקרא בית עולמו שהוא שלו, דהנפש נקראת על שמו שהוא בהשתדלותו זכה לזה. וזה שאמרו זכרונם לברכה (ויקרא רבה פרשה לה): כאלו אתם עשיתם את עצמכם על פסוק "ועשיתם אתם" (ויקרא כו, ג), שעל ידי מעשה התורה ומצות זוכה לזה.

records.targetRef: Sod Yesharim, The Seventh Day of Pesach 10:1
records.themeTitle: The prophet’s lament and the good still to be gathered
records.themeSummary: The fall of a counterpart can narrow a field of service while some good remains for later collection.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim expressly explains the prophet's lament over another nation's fall: the corresponding field of human service becomes smaller when its opposing inclination disappears. Its Egypt example adds that some good remains to be gathered from a distance afterward. This develops the siman's reciprocal powers while preserving the reason for lament and the possibility of later collection.
records.targetEnglish: The matter is like what we find when a prophet foretold a nation's calamity: he lamented, as it says (Isaiah 15:5), ‘My heart cries out for Moav,’ and in chapter 16, ‘My innards sound like a harp for Moav, and my inward parts for Kir Cheres.’ He grieved over the nation's loss, because through this its inclination was annulled, and the power of service corresponding to that particular matter was thereby diminished. Yet in Egypt, although it says (Deuteronomy 17:16), ‘You shall not return by this way again’—even residence in Egypt was forbidden, alluding even to the inanimate—and the Sages said that it was made like a deep place without fish (Berakhot 9b), some points nevertheless remained there that would still enter holiness, to be gathered by Israel from a distance. Of them it says (Psalms 68:32), ‘Nobles will come from Egypt.’ As Pesachim 118b teaches: Egypt will bring a gift to Mashiach. He thinks he should not accept it, but the Holy One tells him to accept it, for they provided lodging for His children in Egypt. Immediately, ‘Nobles will come from Egypt.’
records.originHebrew: וּלְכָךְ יִרְמְיָה קוֹנֵן עַל אָבְדַן אֻמּוֹת עוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "לִבִּי לְמוֹאָב יִזְעָק וְגוֹמֵר" (יְשַׁעְיָה טו, ה; יִרְמְיָה מח, לו), וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּבַמִּדְבָּר רַבָּה (רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת בָּלָק כ, א), וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁבְּאָבְדַן אוֹתָהּ אוּמָּה נִתְבַּטֵּל אוֹתוֹ כֹּחַ (כְּמוֹ שֶׁנִּתְבָּאֵר לְעֵיל אוֹת מ"ז, עַיֵּין שָׁם). וּבְכָל דָּבָר יֵשׁ גַּם כֵּן טוֹב כַּיָּדוּעַ, וְאָז נִתְרוֹמֵם אוֹתוֹ כֹּחַ הַטּוֹב.
records.originEnglish: and therefore Jeremiah lamented over the destruction of gentile nations, as written: "My heart cries out for Moab, etc." (Isaiah 15:5; Jeremiah 48:36), and in Bemidbar Rabbah (beginning of Parashat Balak 20:1), meaning that with the destruction of that nation that spiritual power was abolished (as explained above in Section 47, see there). And within every trait there also resides good as is known, and then that corresponding power of good is exalted.
records.targetHebrew: הענין בזה כמו שמצינו שכאשר התנבא הנביא על פורענות איזה אומה היה מתאונן כענין שנאמר (ישעיהו ט״ו:ה׳) לבי למואב יזעק (ושם ט"ז) מעי למואב ככנור יהמו וקרבי לקיר חרש. שהצטער על אבדן האומה כי עי"ז נתבטל היצר שהי' לזו האומה ממילא נקטן לעומת זה הכח עבודה שנגד זה הפרט. אכן במצרים אף שנאמר (דברים י״ז:ט״ז) לא תוסיפון לשוב בדרך הזה עוד שאף גירות נאסר בארץ מצרים שזה רומז שנאסר אף הדומם. וכן אמרו שעשאה כמצולה שאין בה דגים (ברכות ט':) מ"מ נשאר שם עוד איזה נקודות שיכנסו עוד לקדושה שישראל ילקטו אותם מרחוק שעליהם נאמר (תהילים ס״ח:ל״ב) יאתיו חשמנים מני מצרים וכדאי' (פסחים קי"ח:) עתידה מצרים שתביא דורון למשיח כסבור אינו מקבל מהם א"ל הקב"ה למשיח קבל מהם אכסניא עשו לבניי במצרים מיד יאתיו חשמנים מני מצרים.

records.themeTitle: Different names describe revelation from one source
records.themeSummary: Torah's many divine names concern the powers disclosed to created understanding, while their source remains one.
records.explanation: Sichat Malakhei HaSharet explains the premise behind calling through Torah: a name makes a particular revealed power recognizable, and Torah orders the powers present in creation. The multiplicity belongs to the recipient's apprehension, while the source remains one. This gives content to the siman's distinction between the infinite source beyond names and the divine will expressed in the Torah and its commandments.
records.originHebrew: רַק מִדּוֹתָיו, רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר רְצוֹנוֹ הַמִּתְפַּשֵּׁט בַּבְּרוּאִים, וְהַתּוֹרָה כֻּלָּהּ הִיא כְּלָלוּת רְצוֹנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ. וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ בְּרֵישׁ בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה שֶׁהוּא דְּפוּס מַעֲשֵׂה בְרֵאשִׁית, וּלְכָךְ הִיא שְׁמוֹתָיו, וְלִמּוּדוֹ, דְּהַיְינוּ יְדִיעַת זֶה וְכֵן נִתְקַן בְּבִרְכַּת הַתּוֹרָה: "יוֹדְעֵי שְׁמֶךָ וְלוֹמְדֵי וְכוּלֵי",
records.originEnglish: rather His attributes denote His will expanding within creation, and the entire Torah is the comprehensive embodiment of His blessed will. Therefore they said at the beginning of Bereishit Rabbah that the Torah is the architectural blueprint of Creation; thus it is His Names, and its study—namely the comprehension of this and so was it instituted in the blessing of the Torah: 'those who know Your Name and study, etc.',
records.targetHebrew: אף על פי שבאמת בשרשם הכל אחד יחיד ומיחד כאשר עד שלא נברא העולם, רק להרגשת הנברא יש כאן הרגשת כחות שונות, וכפי כל כח וכח כך הוא נקרא. ולכך כל התורה, שהיא הכוללת סדר כל הכחות הנמצאים בבריאה כמו שנתבאר לעיל, היא כלה שמותיו של השם יתברך, שהוא מקור החיים והקיום לכל אלה הכחות. ובכל כח אנו מכירים שהשם יתברך הוא בעל הכח ההוא, והרי השם יתברך נקרא אצלנו בשם בעל הכח ההוא, וכן בכל פרט; והדברים עמקים ומבארים למשכיל.
records.targetEnglish: In truth, at their root all is one, singular and united, just as before the world was created. Only in the created being's perception is there a perception of different powers, and according to each power He is named. Therefore the entire Torah, which includes the order of all the powers found in creation, consists of the names of Hashem, the source of life and existence for all these powers. Within every power we recognize that Hashem is the master of that power; He is therefore named for us as the master of that power, and so with every particular. These are deep matters, clear to one who understands.

records.themeTitle: Self-scrutiny is not the measure for judging another
records.themeSummary: The responsibility to own one's own deficiency does not authorize assigning the same inward fault to another person.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef reads the encounter with the apparently ugly person as a warning about interpreting another's character. The person must examine himself; the observer must allow for what he cannot see. This clarifies why the present siman places favorable judgment beside the work of finding friends and raising students. The discipline that makes a person demanding of himself need not become suspicion that closes the door to another's Torah growth.
records.originHebrew: דְּעַל תַּלְמִיד שֶׁאֵינוֹ בְּיָדוֹ לֹא שַׁיָּיךְ אַזְהָרָה, רַק שֶׁהוּא מִמֵּילָא, מִי שֶׁעָשָׂה שְׁנֵי דְבָרִים הַקּוֹדְמִים זוֹכֶה אַחַר כָּךְ גַּם כֵּן לְתַלְמִידִים. וּכְלַפֵּי מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ אַנְשֵׁי כְּנֶסֶת הַגְּדוֹלָה: "הַעֲמִידוּ תַלְמִידִים הַרְבֵּה" (אָבוֹת פֶּרֶק א, א), אָמַר הוּא בְּלָשׁוֹן אַחֵר: "הֱוֵי וְכוּלֵי", דְּגַם כֵּן עַל יְדֵי זֶה יִהְיוּ הַרְבֵּה. וּלְפִי שֶׁרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן פְּרַחְיָה הָיָה יוֹצֵאת בִּרְחוֹבוֹתָיו מֵאוֹתוֹ תַּלְמִיד (בְּרָכוֹת יז רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב), וְהָיָה סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ שֶׁלֹּא לְהַרְבּוֹת תַּלְמִידִים, לְפִיכָךְ אָמַר בְּלָשׁוֹן זֶה: לוֹמַר שֶׁאֵין לָחוּשׁ לְכָךְ, וְאַתְּ הֱוֵי דָן וְכוּלֵי, כָּל שֶׁמַּעֲשָׂיו סְתוּמִים, וּבַהֲדֵי כַּבְשֵׁי דְּרַחֲמָנָא לְמָא לָךְ. וְהַלִּמּוּד מֵרַב הוּא הַהַתְחָלָה, וְזֶה נִקְרָא בִּבְרָכוֹת (ו.): אֶחָד שֶׁיּוֹשֵׁב וְעוֹסֵק בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁשְּׁכִינָה עִמּוֹ מִקְּרָא דְּ"אַזְכִּיר אֶת שְׁמִי" (שְׁמוֹת כ, כא), דְּהַתּוֹרָה נִקְרָא שֵׁם ה' כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (שָׁם כא.), וְ"אַזְכִּיר" הַיְינוּ דְּהוּא תּוֹרַת ה' כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל אוֹת קפ"ד, וְנִקְרָא עַל שֵׁם הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁמַּזְכִּיר וּמְלַמֵּד.
records.originEnglish: for regarding students, which is not in his control, an explicit injunction is inapplicable, rather it follows naturally: whoever fulfilled the two preceding directives subsequently merits students as well. And facing what the Men of the Great Assembly said, "Raise up many disciples" (Avot 1:1), Yehoshua ben Perachyah formulated it differently: "Judge favorably," for through this too disciples will multiply. And because Yehoshua ben Perachyah suffered public calamity from that disciple Jesus (Berakhot 17b), and one might think not to multiply students, he therefore taught in this language to show one must not hold back: judge favorably whenever a person's deeds are ambiguous, for why meddle in the hidden ways of the Merciful One? And learning from a master is the beginning, termed in Berakhot 6a "one who sits and engages in Torah, the Shechinah is with him," derived from "wherever I cause My Name to be mentioned" (Exodus 20:21), for Torah is called Hashem's Name (Berakhot 21a), and "cause to be mentioned" means Hashem's Torah as noted in Section 184, named after the Blessed Name Who mentions and teaches it.
records.targetHebrew: אכן זה הוא רק האדם על עצמו, אבל אם רואה הוא בחבירו איזה חסרון אינו רשאי לתלות החסרון בחבירו, רק צריך לדונו לכף זכות, שבודאי האיש הזה במדות הרעות שנראין בו הוא נקי מהם והחטא הוא כשגגה שיוצא מלפני השליט. וזה הענין היה כאן, שר' אלעזר היה רואה באדם שיש בו מדות רעות, והיה דן אותו שבודאי הוא מצידו אינו מבורר ויש לו מדות הרעות. והאדם הזה השיב לו, אף שאני בעצמי מחויב לתלות החסרון בי, אף שמדומה לי שאני מצידי נקי ממדות הרעות, לא כן אתה אין לך רשות לתלות החסרון בי רק לדון אותי לכף זכות, ולך לאומן שעשאני ואמור לו כמה מכוער כלי זה שעשית:
records.targetEnglish: This applies only to a person judging himself. If he sees a deficiency in another, he is not entitled to attribute the deficiency to that person; he must judge him favorably, allowing that the person may be inwardly clear of the bad traits that appear in him and that the failing is like an error proceeding from the ruler. This was the matter here: Rabbi Elazar saw bad traits in a person and judged that the person himself was not refined and possessed those traits. The person answered him: Although I myself must attribute the deficiency to myself, even when it seems to me that I am clear of those bad traits, it is otherwise with you. You are not entitled to attribute the deficiency to me; you must judge me favorably. Go to the Craftsman who made me and say to Him, ‘How ugly is this vessel You made.’
records.translationProvenance: Akiva Publishing original English translation, checked against the complete cited Hebrew paragraph during the comprehensive Tzidkat HaTzadik review; source quotation is separate from the editorial explanation.

records.targetRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 1:31
records.themeTitle: Why the effort to gather has value of its own
records.themeSummary: Limited attainment does not cancel the value of longing and making an effort to come to Torah.
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov uses the same sayings about the reward for hurrying and crowding to learn. It locates their preciousness in the longing and effort of the person, even when the immediate attainment is small. This explains why the siman's least advanced gathering is still beloved, while leaving intact its distinctions among the understanding, responsibilities, and creative work of the four kinds of companions.
records.originHebrew: קפח] אַרְבַּע מַדְרֵגוֹת בַּחֲבֵרִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (שַׁבָּת סג.): מְחַדְּדִים, וְנוֹחִים, וּמַקְשִׁיבִים, וּמַדְגִּילִים; וְהִיא הַפְּחוּתָה, כִּדְמַסַּיֵּים עֲלַהּ: וְהוּא דְּיָדְעֵי, וְהוּא דְּלֵית לְהוּ וְכוּלֵי. וּלְכָךְ נִקְרָא "מַדְגִּילִים" לְפֵירוּשׁ רַשִּׁ"י, שֶׁאֵין בְּיָדָם אֶלָּא הָאֲסִיפָה לְבַד, כְּעִנְיַן "אֲגָרָא דְּפִרְקָא – רִיהֲטָא, וּדְכַלָּה – דּוּחְקָא", שֶׁפֵּירֵשׁ רַשִּׁ"י בִּבְרָכוֹת (ו:) לְפִי שֶׁאֵין מְבִינִים, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
records.originEnglish: There are four levels among colleagues, as written in Shabbat 63a: those who sharpen each other, those who are gentle, those who listen, and those who assemble in groups (madgilim); and the last is the lowest, as the Talmud concludes: provided they know the general form, and provided they have no master in town, etc. And therefore they are called madgilim according to Rashi, having in their power merely assembling together, like "the reward of the public discourse is the running, and of the Kallah gathering is the crowding," which Rashi explains in Berakhot 6b is because many do not understand, see there.
records.targetHebrew: והענין בזה, דהנה דרגא דאברהם אבינו עליו השלום היה כענין שאמרו בש"ס (ברכות ו עמוד ב): "אגרא דכלה – דוחקא; אגרא דפרקא – רהטא", והוא שעיקר היקרות בעולם הזה הוא החשק והרצון לעבודת השם יתברך ויקר הוא מהפעלה עצמה, ואף כי קטן הוא. וכמו שאמר המלך שלמה (קהלת א, א–ב): "הבל הבלים אמר קהלת וגומר", אבל זה ההבל מקיים ומעמיד את העולם, וכדאיתא בזהר הקדוש (ויצא קמו עמוד ב): "האי ספרא אוקים ליה על שבעה הבלים, ועלמא קאים עלייהו"; ועיקר העסק שיש להשם יתברך עם הברואים בעולם הזה הוא החשק והרצון וההשתדלות.
records.targetEnglish: The matter is that Avraham's level was like the Sages' teaching: ‘The reward of the gathering is for the crowding; the reward of the discourse is for hurrying.’ What is chiefly precious in this world is longing and willingness to serve Hashem. It is precious beyond the action itself, even when the action is small. As King Shlomo said, ‘Vanity of vanities, Kohelet said’; yet this breath sustains and establishes the world. The Zohar says that this book was established upon seven breaths, and the world stands upon them. Hashem's principal concern with created beings in this world is their longing, willingness, and effort.
records.translationProvenance: Akiva Publishing original English translation, checked against the complete cited Hebrew paragraph during the comprehensive Tzidkat HaTzadik review; source quotation is separate from the editorial explanation.

records.targetRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayeshev 2
records.themeTitle: Reconciliation requires seeing the other's intention
records.themeSummary: The future removal of envy includes recognition that another person's distinct service is directed toward Heaven.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach explains the very promise about Ephraim cited here through the different roots of Ephraim and Yehudah. Its conclusion places reconciliation in a future clarification of intent: the other is serving Heaven rather than seeking personal pleasure. This develops the siman's demand that the repair of the eye reach the generous heart as well. The source describes that final disclosure; it does not authorize an observer now to presume the inward standing that only Hashem reveals.
records.originHebrew: וְכֵן בִּלְשׁוֹן הַכָּתוּב: "טוֹב עַיִן הוּא יְבֹרָךְ] כִּי נָתַן מִלַּחְמוֹ לַדָּל]" (מִשְׁלֵי כב, ט). וְהַהִיפּוּךְ: עַיִן רָעָה, וּבִלְשׁוֹן הַכָּתוּב "רַע עַיִן" (שָׁם כג, ו). וְזֶה הַחִסָּרוֹן הוּא בְּזַרְעָא דְּיוֹסֵף דַּיְיקָא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "אֶפְרַיִם לֹא יְקַנֵּא אֶת יְהוּדָה]" (יְשַׁעְיָה יא, יג),
records.originEnglish: and so in Scripture: "He that has a bountiful eye shall be blessed, for he gives of his bread to the poor" (Proverbs 22:9). And the opposite is an evil eye, termed in Scripture "evil of eye" (ibid. 23:6). And this vulnerability specifically borders the seed of Joseph, as written: "Ephraim shall not envy Judah" (Isaiah 11:13),
records.targetHebrew: ולזה אלו השני שבטים מתנגדים זה לזה, ולעתיד נאמר "אפרים לא יקנא וכולי ויהודא לא יצור" וכולי, היינו שלאפרים לא יהיה טענה על יהודא במה שיוצא חוץ להלכה ולא יצר לו מזה כי יראה השם יתברך לאפרים את כוונת יהודא שהוא מכוון לשם שמים ולא להנאת עצמו וממילא יהיה שלום ביניהם.
records.targetEnglish: For this reason these two tribes oppose one another. Concerning the future it says, ‘Ephraim will not envy, and Yehudah will not harass.’ Ephraim will have no complaint against Yehudah concerning his going beyond the halakhic line, and will not distress him over it, because Hashem will show Ephraim that Yehudah's intention is directed toward Heaven rather than his own pleasure. Peace will consequently be between them.
records.translationProvenance: Akiva Publishing original English translation, checked against the complete cited Hebrew paragraph during the comprehensive Tzidkat HaTzadik review; source quotation is separate from the editorial explanation.

records.themeTitle: The scholar must recognize Torah within another's conduct
records.themeSummary: An unlearned person's derech eretz can express a Torah inheritance that he cannot yet articulate through study.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim develops the encounter between Rabbi Yannai and an unlearned guest into a responsibility of the scholar. The guest's lack of textual knowledge did not erase the Torah point expressed in his conduct. This clarifies why the present siman distinguishes an am haaretz belonging to the cultivated land from a barren field: the positive inward root must be recognized even where the person cannot himself name it.
records.originHebrew: וּ"בוּר" הוּא שֶׁאֵינוֹ בְּדֶרֶךְ אֶרֶץ, הַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שָׂדֶה בּוּרָה, וְלֹא "שָׂדֶה אֲשֶׁר בֵּרֲכוֹ ה'" (בְּרֵאשִׁית כז, כז) דְּהַיְינוּ חֲקַל תַּפּוּחִין קַדִּישִׁין, דְּהוּא מִדַּת כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהּ זְרִיעַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, שֶׁאֲפִילּוּ רֵיקָנִין שֶׁבָּהּ מְלֵאִים מִצְווֹת וְהַכָּרָה בְּדֶרֶךְ אֶרֶץ וְיִשּׁוּב הָעוֹלָם בֶּאֱמוּנָה שְׁלֵימָה שֶׁהַכֹּל מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ; וְזֶה נִקְרָא "עַם הָאָרֶץ", שֶׁהוּא מִכְּלַל הָאָרֶץ הַיְדוּעָה וְעוֹסֵק בְּדֶרֶךְ אֶרֶץ.
records.originEnglish: And a boor (bur) is one deficient in derekh eretz, like an uncultivated field (sadeh burah), unlike the "field which Hashem has blessed" (Genesis 27:27)—the holy apple orchard, the attribute of Knesset Yisrael bearing the seed of Hashem, whose empty ones are filled with mitzvot and faith that all is from Hashem; and this is called an am ha'aretz (person of the land), being part of the sacred land and engaged in holy derekh eretz.
records.targetHebrew: לכן מי שהוא באמת ת"ח צריך שפיר להכיר מגוון הלבוש של הדרך ארץ שרואה אצל עם הארץ את עומק היקרות מהנקודה של ד"ת הנמצא בו וזה הוא שתפסיה ואמר לו ירותתי גבך וכו' קהלת ינאי לא כתיב כאן אלא קהלת יעקב וכו' היינו שחילק השי"ת את הד"ת לכל נפשות ישראל עד שאינו בנמצא כלל אפילו בהנפש היותר נמוך מישראל שיהיה משולל לגמרי ח"ו מדברי תורה ובזאת הנקודה מד"ת הנמצא גבי כל אחד ואחד הוא באמת מדוגל ומנושא בה יותר מכל ישראל לזה תפסיה לר' ינאי ואמר לו ירותתי גבך כלומר אף שאני בעצמי אינו מכיר הדברי תורה הנמצא בעומק לבי מפני שאני עם הארץ. אבל אתה ר' ינאי הלא תלמיד חכם אתה היה לך להבחין ולהוכיח מהדרך ארץ שיש בי את היקרות מהנקודה של ד"ת הנמצא בי שממנה נסתעף אצלי כל אותו הדרך ארץ ומאלו הדברים האמיתיים נתעורר ר' ינאי והודה מיד לדבריו והתחרט ואמר כל הדא דרך ארץ גבך וקריתך כלבא וכו':
records.targetEnglish: A person who is truly a Torah scholar must therefore recognize, through the outward form of derech eretz he sees in an unlearned person, the deep preciousness of the Torah point within him. This is why the guest seized him and said, ‘My inheritance is with you’: the verse does not say ‘the congregation of Yannai,’ but ‘the congregation of Yaakov.’ Hashem distributed Torah to all the souls of Israel, so that even the lowest soul of Israel is not entirely deprived of Torah, Heaven forbid. In the particular Torah point within each individual he is distinguished and elevated beyond all Israel. The guest therefore said to Rabbi Yannai, ‘My inheritance is with you’—meaning: Although I myself do not recognize the Torah within the depth of my heart because I am unlearned, you, Rabbi Yannai, are a Torah scholar. You should have discerned from my derech eretz the preciousness of the Torah point within me, from which all that conduct branched. These true words awakened Rabbi Yannai; he immediately acknowledged them and regretted his words, saying, ‘You possess all this derech eretz, and I called you a dog.’
records.translationProvenance: Akiva Publishing original English translation, checked against the complete cited Hebrew paragraph during the comprehensive Tzidkat HaTzadik review; source quotation is separate from the editorial explanation.

records.themeTitle: Torah purifies by encompassing the person
records.themeSummary: The comparison to immersion concerns Torah becoming established throughout heart and mind.
records.explanation: Peri Tzadik develops the tents-and-streams teaching with which this siman concludes. The water surrounds the whole body; correspondingly, Torah becomes continuously established in the heart and mind. This explains the positive content of Torah as purification and connects the outward immersion image to a sustained inward formation. It does not collapse the distinct practical categories discussed earlier in the siman.
records.originHebrew: וְגַם אָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (טז רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א): מַקִּישׁ אֹהָלִים לִנְחָלִים וְכוּלֵי, וְהֵם עַצְמָן דּוּגְמַת טְבִילָה:
records.originEnglish: And they also said in Berakhot 16a: tents of Torah are compared to flowing rivers, which themselves function like ritual immersion.
records.targetHebrew: וע"ז הוקשו לנחלים המעלין את האדם מטומאה לטהרה היינו כמו הטובל במים המכסים כל גופו כך על ידי שנקבעו ד"ת בלב ובמוח בתמידות עד שכל שיעור קומתו נטבל כמימי הדעת כדאיתא בהרמב"ם (סוף הלכות מקואות) וע"ז מרמז הזוה"ק דיתדכון ממבועא דנחלא עמיקא. ועל ידי בחי' בינה שבלב שנקבעים הד"ת בלב נפתח לו המקור מרחובות הנהר לטהרת הנפש.
records.targetEnglish: For this reason the tents of Torah were compared to streams that raise a person from impurity to purity. Just as one immerses in water covering the whole body, so words of Torah become permanently established in heart and mind until the person's whole stature is immersed in the waters of knowledge, as the Rambam describes at the end of the laws of immersion pools. This is what the Zohar indicates by purification from the spring of the deep stream. Through the understanding of the heart, in which Torah becomes established, the source from the breadth of the river opens for the purification of the soul.
records.translationProvenance: Akiva Publishing original English translation, checked against the complete cited Hebrew paragraph during the comprehensive Tzidkat HaTzadik review; source quotation is separate from the editorial explanation.

records.targetRef: Sod Yesharim, The First Night of Pesach 27:3
records.themeTitle: Matzah establishes recognition before expansion
records.themeSummary: The initial discipline of matzah can carry recognition of Hashem into the fuller activities that follow.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim develops the same Zohar description of matzah as medicine. The smaller human intervention makes the source easier to recognize, and the first seven days establish a recognition meant to continue when chametz returns. This clarifies the siman's account of matzah opposing the heart's leaven: the aim is an enduring direction within human activity, not simply the disappearance of activity or appetite.
records.originHebrew: וּכְשֶׁהַזֵּיעָה בָּאָה לָאָדָם עַל יְדֵי יִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם, וַדַּאי אֵין לְמַעְלָה הֵימֶנָּה, וְהוּא הֵיפֶךְ מַמָּשׁ לַקֶּרִי כִּדְאִיתָא בַּגְּמָרָא שָׁם. רַק שֶׁזֶּה יָקָר וְקָשֶׁה, וְעַל כָּל פָּנִים קַל הוּא עַל יְדֵי פְּעֻלַּת אָדָם בְּמַעֲשֵׂה הַמִּצְווֹת בְּאֵבָרָיו. וְכָל פְּעֻלַּת מַעֲשֵׂה הַמִּצְווֹת הֲרֵי זֶה קַבָּלַת עוֹל מִצְווֹת וְעוֹל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם וְיִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם.
records.originEnglish: And when sweat comes to a person through fear of Heaven, there is certainly nothing higher, being the absolute opposite of seminal emission as stated in the Gemara. But that is rare and difficult, whereas it is accessible through a person's physical labor in performing mitzvot with his limbs. And all physical execution of mitzvot constitutes the acceptance of the yoke of commandments, the yoke of Heaven, and fear of God.
records.targetHebrew: מצה זו שאנו אוכלים על שום מה על שום שלא הספיק בצקת של אבותינו להחמיץ וכו' ענין מצה מורה על מעט פעולת אדם ובזה הוא בניקל עדיין להכיר את השורש אבל חמץ רומז על הרבה פעולת אדם וזה מסתיר את השורש כי במקום שיש בו פעולת אדם ביותר שם אין עוד כ"כ הכרה בהשורש כענין איסור כלאים שמערבב דעת אדם ומסתיר הכרתו ולזה כאן בההתחלה נצטוו ישראל במצה לקבוע בלבבם הכרת השורש והוא כדאיתא בזוה"ק (תצוה קפ"ג:) כד נפקי ישראל ממצרים לא הוו ידעו עיקרא ורזא דמהימנותא אמר קב"ה יטעמון ישראל אסוותא דא ועד דייכלין אסוותא דא לא אתחזו להון מיכלא אחרא כיון דאכלו מצה דאיהו אסוותא למיעל ולמנדע ברזא דמהימנותא אמר קב"ה מכאן ולהלאה אתחזי לון חמץ וייכלון לי' דהא לא יכול לניקא לון וכו' וזה הוא כענין שנצטוו ישראל למסור בחזרה להשי"ת כל הראשית כגון תרומה ומעשרות וחלה שנקראו ראשית דגנך וגו' והוא כי ע"י שמכיר האדם בהשורש ית' בהתחלה בזה שממליך עליו הש"י בראשית ההשפעה ששופע הש"י אז מקנה לו הש"י כל הנשאר שיזכ' בה האד' משלחן גבוה כך צריכין ישראל לברר א"ע בהכרת השורש באלו הז' ימים ע"י אכילת מצה כי אלו ז' ימים הם ההתחלה ומפאת זה יהי' להאדם הכרה גם בכל השנה אף כשיאכל חמץ יהי' נמי מכיר את אורו ית' בכל ההשפעות:
records.targetEnglish: ‘This matzah that we eat—why? Because our ancestors' dough did not have time to become leavened.’ Matzah indicates a small degree of human action, through which it is still easy to recognize the source. Chametz indicates more human action, which can conceal the source, as when the mixing of a person's own understanding obscures recognition. At the beginning Israel were therefore commanded concerning matzah to establish recognition of the source in their hearts. The Zohar says that when Israel left Egypt they did not know the root and secret of faith. Hashem said: Let Israel taste this medicine; while they eat it, no other food should be shown to them. Once they ate matzah, the medicine for entering and knowing the secret of faith, Hashem said: From now on chametz is fitting for them and cannot harm them. This resembles the command to return every first portion to Hashem, such as terumah, tithes and challah. When a person recognizes the source at the beginning and accepts Hashem's kingship at the start of an outpouring, Hashem grants him the remainder to receive from the divine table. So Israel must clarify their recognition of the source during these first seven days through eating matzah. Through this they can recognize His light in every gift throughout the year, even when eating chametz.
records.translationProvenance: Akiva Publishing original English translation, checked against the complete cited Hebrew paragraph during the comprehensive Tzidkat HaTzadik review; source quotation is separate from the editorial explanation.

records.themeTitle: Related life does not erase the difference between person and object
records.themeSummary: A possession can have a real relation to a person's life while remaining a distinct kind of created thing.
records.explanation: Kometz HaMinchah explains the premise behind holiness extending into possessions: the divine word sustains both the person and the object, and the powers within the person correspond to levels of created life. It explicitly preserves the difference between them. This helps the reader understand the present siman's extension of love into possessions without mistaking that relation for an assertion that every object is already a human soul or that every owner has reached this exceptional degree of holiness.
records.originHebrew: וּשְׁנֵי אֵלּוּ עֲדַיִן הוּא בְּיַד עֲבוֹדַת הָאָדָם וְהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ לְהַשִּׂיג לָזֶה; וּלְכָךְ בְּפָרָשַׁת "וְהָיָה אִם שָׁמֹעַ" (דְּבָרִים יא, יג) שֶׁאָמַר "וּלְעָבְדוֹ", נִזְכַּר רַק שְׁנֵי אֵלֶּה, מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן "בְּכָל מְאֹדְךָ" אֵינוֹ בְּיַד עֲבוֹדַת הָאָדָם, רַק מִסַּיַּעְתָּא דִּשְׁמַיָּא,
records.originEnglish: And these two levels are still within the grasp of human service and effort to attain; and therefore in the second paragraph of Shema where it says "and to serve Him," only these two are mentioned ("with all your heart and with all your soul"), whereas "with all your might (me'odekha)" is not solely within human effort, but depends on Heavenly assistance,
records.targetHebrew: הרכוש שייך לאדם, שהרי גם כשנאבד מידו צריך להחזיר כשיש לו סימן או טביעות עין, שרצה לומר: איזה שייכות, הכרה, ועדות שהוא שלו. והיינו כי הכל בדבר ה' המחיהו, ומסתמא יש לאותו חיים שלו שייכות באותם חיים; כי ד' ארבע מדרגות הם: דומם, צומח, חי, מדבר בעולם השפל, והחמישית הם העליונים; וכן ד' ארבעה יסודות: אש, רוח, מים, עפר, ושמים – גשם חמישי; וכן ד' ארבע נפשות: נפש, רוח, נשמה, ונשמה לנשמה חיה, והחמישית – יחידה, כמו שכתבתי כל זה במקום אחר. והיינו שבאדם מורכב כל דומם, צומח, חי, מדבר, וכח הדומם הוא כח הנפש וכולי; ובודאי שיש חילוק בין כח הדומם שבדומם לכח הדומם שבאדם, אבל מכל מקום יש להם חבור ושייכות.
records.targetEnglish: Possessions belong to a person: even after they are lost they must be returned when he has an identifying mark or recognition, indicating a relation, recognition and testimony that they are his. Everything exists through the word of Hashem that gives it life, and a person's life must have a relation to that life. There are four levels in the lower world—inanimate, growing, living and speaking—and the fifth is the higher beings. Correspondingly there are four elements—fire, air, water and earth—with heaven as the fifth substance; and four soul levels—nefesh, ruach, neshamah and the soul of the soul, chayah—with yechidah as the fifth. The human being includes the inanimate, growing, living and speaking levels, and the inanimate power corresponds to nefesh. Certainly there is a difference between the inanimate power in an inanimate object and that power within a person; nevertheless they have a connection and relation.
records.translationProvenance: Akiva Publishing original English translation, checked against the complete cited Hebrew paragraph during the comprehensive Tzidkat HaTzadik review; source quotation is separate from the editorial explanation.

records.themeTitle: One coin holds love and awe together
records.themeSummary: The union of love and awe is more stable than an alternation between youthful excitement and aged restraint.
records.explanation: Kometz HaMinchah uses Avraham's coin to describe love and awe existing within one whole. The image helps explain the present siman's demand for love that remains even in darkness and distress: the purpose is not to eliminate awe, but to prevent either condition from excluding the other. It also preserves the distinction between a passing intensity of love and the union that continues through changing circumstances.
records.originHebrew: וְגַם יֵשׁ חִלּוּק לָאָדָם: כְּשֶׁהוּא בְּשִׂמְחָה וְנִיחָא אָז גּוֹבֵר מִדַּת אַהֲבָה, וּבְצַעַר וְצָרָה – מִדַּת הַיִּרְאָה; וּבֶאֱמֶת צָרִיךְ לְאַהֲבָה בֵּין בְּטִיבוּ בֵּין בְּעָקוּ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּהַקְדָּמַת הַזֹּהַר (יב עַמּוּד א). וְזֶה נִדְרַשׁ בִּבְרָכוֹת (נד.) מִ"בְּכָל מְאֹדְךָ", שֶׁהוּא נֶגֶד יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁהוּא הָיָה כּוֹלֵל שְׁתֵּי הַמִּדּוֹת בְּכָל זְמַן, כִּדְבָרֵי שַׁמַּאי בְּתַנָּא דְבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ (סֵדֶר אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה רֵישׁ פֶּרֶק ג): אֲנִי יָרֵאתִי מִתּוֹךְ שִׂמְחָתִי וְשָׂמַחְתִּי מִתּוֹךְ יִרְאָתִי. וְלָכֵן אוֹמְרִים בְּעַרְבִית "אַהֲבַת עוֹלָם" נֶגֶד יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁתִּיקֵּן תְּפִלַּת עַרְבִית, וְהוּא מִדָּתוֹ: לִהְיוֹת גַּם בָּעֶרֶב וְעֵת חֶשְׁכַּת הַצָּרוֹת הָאַהֲבָה בִּלְתִּי נִיתֶּקֶת. וּבְשַׁחֲרִית – בֹּקֶר דְּאַבְרָהָם שֶׁתִּיקֵּן תְּפִלַּת שַׁחֲרִית – "אַהֲבָה רַבָּה" כְּמִדָּתוֹ, כִּי בְּאוֹר הַיּוֹם הַמֵּאִיר וּבָא לְלִבּוֹת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מִתְלַהֵב הַלֵּב בְּאַהֲבָה רַבָּה לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וּמִדָּה כְּנֶגֶד מִדָּה: אַהֲבָה רַבָּה אֲהַבְתָּנוּ וְכוּלֵי.
records.originEnglish: and there is a distinction in man: when in joy and tranquility love surges, while in sorrow and distress awe dominates; and in truth one must love both in prosperity and in adversity, as written in the Zohar's introduction (12a). And this is derived in Berakhot 54a from "with all your might," which corresponds to our father Jacob who integrated both traits at all times, as in Tanna DeBei Eliyahu: "I feared out of my joy, and rejoiced out of my fear." Therefore we recite in the evening service Ahavat Olam facing Jacob who instituted Maariv, his trait being that even in the evening darkness of distress love remains unsevered. And in Shacharit—the morning of Abraham who instituted Shacharit—we recite Ahavah Rabbah reflecting his trait, for in the daylight shining into Jewish hearts the heart burns with intense love for Hashem, and measure for measure: "With a great love have You loved us, etc."
records.targetHebrew: וידוע האהבה בימי הנעורים, מה שאין כן בימי הזקנה: קהלת יב, ה "ותפר האביונה"; וכידוע דשלמה המלך עליו השלום, בילדותו אמר שיר השירים – תוקף אהבה, ובזקנותו קהלת – תוקף היראה. אבל אברהם חדש וקבע למטבע היוצאת דבר זה: שיהיה על מטבע אחת זקן וזקנה מכאן, ובחור ובתולה מכאן הכל מיוחד ביחוד גמור, האהבה ויראה.
records.targetEnglish: Love is characteristic of youth, unlike old age, when ‘desire fails.’ As is known, Shlomo in his youth composed Shir HaShirim, the intensity of love, and in his old age Kohelet, the intensity of awe. Avraham, however, established something new in the circulating coin: on one coin, an old man and woman on one side, and a young man and maiden on the other, all united in a complete union—love and awe.
records.translationProvenance: Akiva Publishing original English translation, checked against the complete cited Hebrew paragraph during the comprehensive Tzidkat HaTzadik review; source quotation is separate from the editorial explanation.

records.themeTitle: Surrender can reach even one's expected spiritual legacy
records.themeSummary: Avraham's devotion is described as relinquishing his expected continuation in both worlds.
records.explanation: In the preceding paragraph Beit Yaakov explains that Avraham's readiness to offer his only son seemed to leave him without reward or enduring continuation. The quoted conclusion therefore describes self-giving in two worlds, not bodily courage alone. This makes the opening of the present siman concrete: the attachment being yielded can include one's expectation of spiritual attainment and legacy. The illustration remains Avraham's response to a divine command.
records.originHebrew: רא] מְסִירַת נֶפֶשׁ בִּשְׁבִיל אַהֲבַת ה' אֵינוֹ הַנֶּפֶשׁ לְבַד כִּפְשָׁטֵיהּ, אֶלָּא גַּם הַנְּשָׁמָה,
records.originEnglish: Surrendering one's life (mesirut nefesh) for the love of Hashem is not limited to the bodily life (nefesh) alone, but includes the soul (neshamah),
records.targetHebrew: והוא לא הביט על כל זה והשליך נפשו מנגד בשביל אהבת השם יתברך, והיה מוסר נפשו בשני עולמות, שהסכים שלא ישאר ממנו שום השארה, והוא רק למען אהבתו להשם יתברך, לכן שכרו כפול ומכופל.
records.targetEnglish: He did not look to any of this, but cast his life aside for love of Hashem. He surrendered himself in both worlds, agreeing that no continuation of himself should remain, solely for love of Hashem. His reward is therefore doubled and multiplied.
records.translationProvenance: Akiva Publishing original English translation, checked against the complete cited Hebrew paragraph during the comprehensive Tzidkat HaTzadik review; source quotation is separate from the editorial explanation.

records.themeTitle: The third stage discloses the unity of the earlier stages
records.themeSummary: Settled understanding recognizes the place of both initial kindness and the discipline of concealment.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains the third dimension as a return, through one's work, to the first kindness. The intervening severity had seemed to oppose the light, but the completed understanding sees why concealment allowed meaningful service. This clarifies the siman's final distinction: love and awe are necessary powers of service, while the complete human form is a settled direction toward Hashem's will that can hold them together.
records.originHebrew: וּלְכָךְ צוּרַת יַעֲקֹב חֲקוּקָה בְּכִסֵּא הַכָּבוֹד, שֶׁהוּא נֶגֶד שֵׁם הֲוָיָ"ה שֶׁהוּא הַכּוֹלֵל הַכֹּל כַּנּוֹדָע. כִּי זֶה כָּל הָאָדָם: לִהְיוֹת נִמְשָׁךְ אַחַר אֲמִיתַּת רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּלִי שׁוּם מָסָךְ וּמוֹנֵעַ; רַק שֶׁהַדֶּרֶךְ לְהַגִּיעַ לָזֶה הוּא עַל יְדֵי אַהֲבָה וְיִרְאָה הַקּוֹדְמִין:
records.originEnglish: Therefore the image of Jacob is engraved upon the Throne of Glory, corresponding to the Name Havayah which encompasses all, as is known. For this is the whole duty of man: to be drawn after the absolute truth of the will of Hashem without any barrier or hindrance; only that the path to reach this is through the preceding love and fear.
records.targetHebrew: כי תליתאי נקרא אחר שבא האדם בחזרה אל החסד הראשון על ידי עבודתו. ואף שאיתא בזוה"ק (קדושים פ:) אורייתא מסטרא דגבורה נפקת, זה הכל קודם שבוקע את ההעלם, אז נדמה לו שאורו של השי"ת וההעלם הם שני הפכיים, וזה מורה מסטרא דגבורה נפקת, אבל אח"כ רואה באמת שהכל הוא בחסדו, שגם ההעלם הזה הוא מחמת שהשי"ת הוא רב חסד, ורצה שיהיה לאדם חלק בעבודתו אשר הוא עובד, לזה העלים השי"ת ממנו את החסד הזה כדי שיהיה מקום לעבודה ואז נקרא אוריאן תליתאי.
records.targetEnglish: The third stage is named when a person returns through his service to the first kindness. Although the Zohar says that Torah issues from the side of severity, this concerns the stage before he breaks through the concealment. Then Hashem's light and the concealment appear to him as opposites. Afterward he truly sees that all is through His kindness: the concealment too exists because Hashem abounds in kindness and wanted the person to have a share in the service he performs. He therefore concealed that kindness so there would be room for service. This is then called threefold Torah.
records.translationProvenance: Akiva Publishing original English translation, checked against the complete cited Hebrew paragraph during the comprehensive Tzidkat HaTzadik review; source quotation is separate from the editorial explanation.

records.themeTitle: The cry of humility differs from giving up
records.themeSummary: Recognizing a fall can reopen service; concluding that repentance is closed prolongs the temptation.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim distinguishes the temptation toward an act from the later temptation to despair after its pleasure has ended. This adds an essential qualification to the siman's sequence of a broken vessel, recognized smallness, and a renewed cry. Humility makes room for help and repair; it is not the judgment that further return is impossible.
records.originHebrew: וְנַעֲשָׂה בֶּאֱמֶת מֶלֶךְ בִּישֻׁרוּן כִּי אַחַר הַתִּיקּוּן נִתְרַחֲבוּ כָּל הַכֵּלִים כַּנּוֹדָע. וְהַיְינוּ דְּהַגַּאֲוָה הוּא שֶׁרוֹצֶה לְקַבֵּל דָּבָר שֶׁאֵין יָכוֹל לִיכָּנֵס בַּכְּלִי שֶׁלּוֹ, שֶׁאֵינוֹ כְּלִי קִבּוּל כָּל כָּךְ טוֹבָה וְשֶׁפַע, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה נִשְׁבָּר חַס וְשָׁלוֹם. וְעַל יְדֵי הַשְּׁבִירָה מַכִּיר שִׁפְלוּתוֹ אַחַר שֶׁכְּבָר טָעַם מִן הָאוֹר וְנֶעְלַם מִמֶּנּוּ, עַל יְדֵי זֶה בָּא לַעֲנָוָה גְּדוֹלָה וְנוֹלָד שֵׁם מַ"ה הֶחָדָשׁ הַמְּתַקֵּן הַכֵּלִים וּמַרְחִיבָן לְקַבֵּל בֶּאֱמֶת כָּל כָּךְ.
records.originEnglish: becoming truly king in Jeshurun, for after rectification all vessels were expanded. That is, pride consists of seeking to receive what cannot fit into one's vessel, not being a vessel fit for such immense light, breaking as a result. And through the shattering he recognizes his lowliness after having tasted the light and lost it, arriving at profound humility, birthing the new Name Mah which heals the vessels and expands them to receive.
records.targetHebrew: היינו מה שהאדם מייאש א"ע ונדמה לו שאתמנע תשובה מני' זה מזיק לאדם ביותר ועל זה רמזו ז"ל בגמ' (ב"מ קז:) הכל ברוח כו' אי לאו זיקא עבדי להו סמא וחיי וזה הגמר נקרא ג"כ דכר ואז מתיצב ג"כ עמלק לקטרג וזהו ראשית גוים עמלק היינו שההתחלה נמשך ממנו. ואחריתו עדי אובד היינו שבהגמר מתיצב נמי עמלק להכניס התרשלות ומיחושים בלב אדם שאתמנע תשובה ממנו ח"ו:
records.targetEnglish: When a person despairs of himself and imagines that repentance has been withheld from him, this harms him most of all. The Sages alluded to this when they said that everything depends on the wind: were it not for the wind, they could make a remedy and live. This final stage too is called masculine, and Amalek again stands to accuse. ‘The first of nations is Amalek’ means that the beginning is drawn from him. ‘Its end is destruction’ means that at the conclusion Amalek again stands to introduce slackness and anxious suspicions into a person's heart, as though repentance had been withheld from him, Heaven forbid.
records.translationProvenance: Akiva Publishing original English translation, checked against the complete cited Hebrew paragraph during the comprehensive Tzidkat HaTzadik review; source quotation is separate from the editorial explanation.

records.targetRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 14:7
records.themeTitle: A fixed view can become a house of slavery
records.themeSummary: The Exodus frees a person from treating one enjoyment or opinion as the whole of his life.
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov explains why leaving Egypt is more than receiving an argument about the Creator. A person can feel unable to leave an enjoyment or a fixed conception because it seems to constitute his life. Freedom makes him ready to follow Hashem's will afresh. This gives a concrete meaning to the present siman's contrast between constricting imagination and the enduring recognition established through the Exodus.
records.originHebrew: רז] דִּמְיוֹנוֹת שָׁוְא הֵם חוֹצְצִים בִּפְנֵי יְדִיעַת אֱלֹהוּת וְהַכָּרָתוֹ מִלְּהִכָּנֵס בַּלֵּב. וְלָכֵן אָמַר פַּרְעֹה, שֶׁהוּא מֶלֶךְ מִצְרַיִם וּבוֹ תֹּקֶף הַשְּׁקִיעוּת בַּדִּמְיוֹן: "לֹא יָדַעְתִּי אֶת ה'" (שְׁמוֹת ה, ב). וְהַתְחָלַת "אָנֹכִי [ה' אֱלֹהֶיךָ] אֲשֶׁר הוֹצֵאתִיךָ מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם]" (שָׁם כ, ב), וְאֵין זֶה טַעַם אוֹ מוֹפֵת, דְּאִם כֵּן הֲוָה לֵיהּ לְמֵימַר: אֲשֶׁר בָּרָאתִי שָׁמַיִם וָאָרֶץ אוֹ בְּרָאתִיךָ. רַק כִּי "אָנֹכִי" אֵין מַתְחִיל בִּלְשׁוֹן מִצְוָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר, דְּזֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְצַוּוֹת וּלְהַזְהִיר, כִּי מִי שֶׁאֵין מַאֲמִין כְּלָל מַה יּוֹעִיל הַצִּוּוּי; וּכְעִנְיַן פַּרְעֹה שֶׁאָמַר "לֹא יָדַעְתִּי", אָמְרוּ עָלָיו (שְׁמוֹת רַבָּה סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה ג): בִּדְבָרִים לֹא יִוָּסֶר עָבֶד, רַק שֵׁבֶט וְכוּלֵי.
records.originEnglish: Vain imaginations and false delusions act as a barrier preventing the knowledge and awareness of Godliness from penetrating into the heart. And therefore Pharaoh, who was the king of Egypt and embodied the ultimate immersion in delusion, declared: "I know not Hashem" (Exodus 5:2). And the Decalogue opens with "I am Hashem your God, Who brought you out of the land of Egypt" (Exodus 20:2), which is neither an intellectual proof nor a rationale, for were that so, Scripture should have said: "Who created heaven and earth" or "Who created you." Rather, "I am" does not open in the language of a formal commandment, as I wrote elsewhere, for over fundamental belief it is impossible to issue a command or warning, since for one who does not believe at all, what will a command avail? and like Pharaoh who stated "I know not," concerning whom our Sages expounded (Shemot Rabbah 3): "A servant will not be corrected by words" (Proverbs 29:19), but only with a rod, etc.
records.targetHebrew: [א] "לֶךְ לְךָ" הוּא כְּנֶגֶד (יִתְרוֹ כ, ב): "אָנֹכִי ה' אֱלֹהֶיךָ אֲשֶׁר הוֹצֵאתִיךָ מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם": שֶׁיְּצִיאַת מִצְרַיִם הָיְתָה שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל מְשׁוּקָּעִים עוֹד בְּשׁוּם דָּבָר; שֶׁכֵּן נִמְצָא לִפְעָמִים שֶׁהָאָדָם מְשׁוּקָּע בַּהֲנָאוֹת וְתַאֲווֹת קְטַנּוֹת וְאֵין בְּכֹחוֹ לְהִפָּרֵד מֵהֶם, מִפְּנֵי שֶׁנִּרְאֶה לוֹ שֶׁהֵם חַיָּיו, וְכֵן הָיוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל מְשׁוּקָּעִים בְּמִצְרַיִם. וּכְעִנְיַן דְּאִיתָא (מְכִילְתָּא יִתְרוֹ) שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה עֶבֶד יָכוֹל לִבְרוֹחַ מִמִּצְרַיִם, וְהוּא מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהָיָה נִדְמֶה לוֹ שֶׁטּוֹב לוֹ לַעֲבוֹד אֶת מִצְרַיִם מִלִּהְיוֹת שַׂר בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר. וְכֵן נִמְצָא לִפְעָמִים שֶׁאָדָם מְשׁוּקָּע בְּשֵׂכֶל וְדֵעָה אַחַת וְלֹא יוּכַל לָזוּז מִמֶּנָּה; וְזֶה הָיָה עִיקַּר גָּלוּת מִצְרַיִם, שֶׁהָיָה לָהֶם נִיחָא מִזֶּה שֶׁהֵם עֲבָדִים, וְהָיָה נִדְמֶה לָהֶם שֶׁמֵּעוֹלָם הֵם עֲבָדִים, וְזֶהוּ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "אֲשֶׁר הוֹצֵאתִיךָ מִבֵּית עֲבָדִים". וְאָכֵן אֵין הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ חָפֵץ בָּזֶה שֶׁהָאָדָם יִהְיֶה כָּפוּף תַּחַת דֵּעָה אַחַת וְיִתְעַקֵּשׁ בָּהּ לְבַל יָזוּז מִמֶּנָּה; אֲבָל בָּזֶה חָפֵץ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ: שֶׁהָאָדָם יִהְיֶה נָכוֹן בְּכָל רֶגַע לְהִמָּשֵׁךְ רַק אַחַר רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
records.targetEnglish: ‘Go forth’ corresponds to ‘I am Hashem your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.’ The Exodus meant that Israel should no longer be sunk in any one thing. Sometimes a person is immersed in small pleasures and desires and cannot separate from them because they appear to him to be his life; so Israel were immersed in Egypt. The Sages teach that no slave could escape Egypt: it seemed better to him to serve Egypt than to be a ruler elsewhere. Similarly, a person can be immersed in one conception or opinion and unable to move from it. This was the principal Egyptian exile: they were content to be slaves and imagined they had always been slaves. Hence, ‘who brought you out of the house of slaves.’ Hashem does not desire a person to be bent beneath one opinion, stubbornly refusing to move from it. He desires the person to be ready at every moment to follow only His will.
records.translationProvenance: Akiva Publishing original English translation, checked against the complete cited Hebrew paragraph during the comprehensive Tzidkat HaTzadik review; source quotation is separate from the editorial explanation.

records.themeTitle: The request for speech begins with acknowledged lordship
records.themeSummary: Prayer is traced to the divine kingship whose authority the person accepts.
records.explanation: Kometz HaMinchah connects David's ‘I am prayer’ to the request ‘Adonai, open my lips.’ Accepting divine lordship allows speech to become an expression of that relation. This illuminates the siman's distinction between a mouth moving on its own and speech opened from the heart. The full attained condition is a model toward which the ordinary opening request turns, rather than something proved merely by pronouncing its words.
records.originHebrew: אֲבָל תָּמִיד לָא צְרִיכֵי כַּוָּנָה כְּלָל, דְּמִמֵּילָא צָעַק לִבָּם אֶל ה' בְּעֵת הַתְּפִלָּה בְּמִי שֶׁאֵינוֹ בַּעַל דִּמְיוֹן. אֲבָל בְּכָל אָדָם כִּמְעַט אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהִנָּצֵל כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל. וְעַל זֶה תִּקְּנוּ בַּתְּחִלָּה: "אֲדֹנָי שְׂפָתַי תִּפְתָּח וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים נא, יז), שֶׁהַשֵּׁם אֲדֹנָ"י מוֹרֶה עַל שְׁכִינָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁבְּקֶרֶב לִבּוֹת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל;
records.originEnglish: But ordinarily they required no deliberate effort at all, their heart crying out spontaneously to Hashem during prayer, as is true of anyone free from delusion. But for ordinary man it is virtually impossible to be spared from this, as noted above. And for this reason they instituted at the opening: "O Lord, open my lips, etc." (Psalms 51:17), for the Name Adonai alludes to His Shechinah dwelling within the hearts of the children of Israel;
records.targetHebrew: ומאמר "והיה ברכה" כמאמר "ואני תפלה" תהלים קט, ד דדוד המלך עליו השלום, שהוא עצמו עצם התפלה הנמשך ממקור מלכותו ואדונותו, כמו שכתוב שם נא, יז: "אדני שפתי תפתח", שהוא עולם הדבור כידוע וכמו שכתוב בתיקונים; וכשמקבל אדונותו באמת גמור, אז נעשה מרכבה לאותה מדה ומתכלל.
records.targetEnglish: The statement ‘Be a blessing’ is like David's statement ‘I am prayer’: he himself is the very prayer flowing from the source of His kingship and lordship. As it says, ‘Adonai, open my lips,’ which is the world of speech, as is known and as stated in Tikkunim. When a person accepts His lordship in complete truth, he becomes a vehicle for that attribute and is included within it.
records.translationProvenance: Akiva Publishing original English translation, checked against the complete cited Hebrew paragraph during the comprehensive Tzidkat HaTzadik review; source quotation is separate from the editorial explanation.

records.themeTitle: The change is in receiving the gift
records.themeSummary: Prayer's movement from severity to mercy need not mean a change in Hashem's will to give.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef asks how the Sages can describe righteous prayer as changing the divine measure when Hashem does not change. Its answer locates the change in the recipient's attainment of the gift. This illuminates the present siman's language that Hashem Himself desires the requested fulfillment and waits for prayer. The petition opens a relation of reception; it is not portrayed as persuading an unwilling giver to acquire a new disposition.
records.originHebrew: וְעַל יְדֵי תּוֹרָה מִיָּד הוּא הַשְׁלָמַת הַחִסָּרוֹן, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "פִּקּוּדֵי ה' יְשָׁרִים] מְשַׂמְּחֵי לֵב" (תְּהִלִּים יט, ט), וְשִׂמְחָה הוּא הִיפּוּךְ הַיִּרְאָה. אֲבָל עַל יְדֵי תְּפִלָּה, אִם הוּא כִּדְבָרֵי שַׁמַּאי (תַּעֲנִית כה סוֹף עַמּוּד ב): אָמַר מַשִּׁיב הָרוּחַ – נָשֵׁיב זִיקָא וְכוּלֵי, עַל זֶה אָמַר: "וְשִׂמַּחְתִּים בְּבֵית תְּפִלָּתִי" (יְשַׁעְיָה נו, ז), שֶׁמִּיָּד מַגִּיעַ הַמִּלּוּי;
records.originEnglish: And through Torah the replenishment of deficiency is immediate, as written: "The statutes of Hashem are right, rejoicing the heart" (Psalms 19:9), and joy is the opposite of fear. But through prayer, if it is like the saying in Ta'anit 25b: when he recited "He causes the wind to blow," the wind blew, etc., concerning this Scripture states: "and make them joyful in My house of prayer" (Isaiah 56:7), for fulfillment arrives immediately;
records.targetHebrew: ובאמת מצד השי"ת אין שום השתנות כדכתיב (מלאכי ג׳:ו׳) אני ד' לא שניתי, ורק כל השינוי הוא מצד המקבל. כי השפע של השי"ת לא נפסק לעולם. ורק מצד המקבל נדמה לפעמים שנפסק, וע"י תפילתו משיג השפע.
records.targetEnglish: In truth, from Hashem's side there is no change, as it says, ‘I, Hashem, have not changed.’ All the change is on the recipient's side. Hashem's outpouring never ceases. Only from the recipient's side does it sometimes appear to have ceased; through his prayer he attains that outpouring.
records.translationProvenance: Akiva Publishing original English translation, checked against the complete cited Hebrew paragraph during the comprehensive Tzidkat HaTzadik review; source quotation is separate from the editorial explanation.

records.themeTitle: The poor person's speech overflows from felt need
records.themeSummary: The description of unarranged prayer concerns a heart whose lack cannot remain unspoken.
records.explanation: Et HaOchel develops the same Psalm and the comparison to Channah. Its larger context defines the soul's poverty as acknowledging that it has nothing independently and lives through heavenly mercy. The quoted passage explains why such a prayer can emerge as poured-out speech rather than a polished arrangement. This supports the siman's emphasis on the heart's reality, without making disorder of words a substitute for that reality.
records.originHebrew: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ג, קצה עַמּוּד א) דִּתְפִלָּה דְּעָנִי כְּלַל כָּל צְלוֹתִין וּבָקְעֵי רְקִיעִין. וְאֵין עָנִי אֶלָּא בְּדַעַת (נְדָרִים מא.), אֲפִילּוּ אֵין יוֹדֵעַ אֵיךְ לְהִתְפַּלֵּל וּלְרַצּוֹת לְקוֹנוֹ,
records.originEnglish: and as written in the Zohar (Part III, 195a) that the prayer of the afflicted man encompasses all prayers and cleaves through the heavens. And "poor" denotes poor in knowledge (Nedarim 41a), even one who does not know how to pray properly and find favor before his Maker;
records.targetHebrew: ועל זה הוא אכילת לחם עני, כטעם "תפלה לעני כי יעטף" [תהלים ק״ב:א׳] דעטיף כל צלותין ובקע רקיעין, כי העני מגדל חסרונו ישפך שיחו בשפיכת נפשו כדרך "ותשפך את נפשה" דחנה, ולא יוכל לכלכל בלב עד כי ידבר בפה וירעיש בקול. ובכח אותה האכילה להוליד כח הדבורין היוצאין מלב, ועקר החיות כפי גדל העני והרגשת המצאון;
records.targetEnglish: This is the meaning of eating the bread of poverty, like ‘A prayer of the poor person when he is overwhelmed,’ which envelops all prayers and breaks through the heavens. Because of his great lack, the poor person pours out his speech as the pouring out of his soul, like Channah pouring out her soul. He cannot contain it within his heart, until he speaks with his mouth and raises his voice. That eating has the power to bring forth speech that issues from the heart; the principal vitality is in proportion to the depth of the poverty and the felt need.
records.translationProvenance: Akiva Publishing original English translation, checked against the complete cited Hebrew paragraph during the comprehensive Tzidkat HaTzadik review; source quotation is separate from the editorial explanation.

records.targetRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Lech Lecha 5
records.themeTitle: Receiving more also enlarges the work of reception
records.themeSummary: Passing the trial of lack does not remove the need to receive abundance with care.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach reads Avraham's wealth as a new burden of responsibility after the trial of poverty, using the same prayer from Proverbs cited here. Its material setting illustrates the siman's more general distinction: more of a gift is not automatically better unless the recipient can hold it properly. Asking for an enlarged vessel therefore accompanies asking for a greater Torah blessing.
records.originHebrew: [ריד] כְּשֶׁאָדָם מְבַקֵּשׁ עַל מַעֲלָה, יֵשׁ לוֹ לְבַקֵּשׁ שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה יוֹתֵר מִגְּבוּלוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "שָׁוְא וּדְבַר כָּזָב הַרְחֵק מִמֶּנִּי" (מִשְׁלֵי ל, ח). פֵּירוּשׁ, "שָׁוְא" – דִּמְיוֹנוֹת שֶׁל תֹּהוּ, וְ"דָבָר" הַיְינוּ דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל אוֹת קפ"ג מִגְּמָרָא דְּתַעֲנִית (י:); וַאֲפִילּוּ דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, רַק שֶׁהוּא לְמַעְלָה מִגְּבוּלוֹ, וַהֲרֵי זֶה כּוֹזֵב וּפוֹסֵק – הַרְחֵק. וְסִיֵּים עַל זֶה: "רֵאשׁ וָעֹשֶׁר אַל תִּתֶּן לִי]... פֶּן אֶשְׂבַּע וְכִחַשְׁתִּי וְגוֹמֵר" (שָׁם, ח–ט), שֶׁכְּשֶׁיַּעֲלֶה בְּמַדְרֵגוֹת שֶׁאֵינָם לְפִי עֵרֶךְ כְּלִי קִבּוּלוֹ, יָבוֹא לְגַאֲוָה וּלְשֶׁקֶר חַס וְשָׁלוֹם. וְעַל זֶה בִּקֵּשׁ יַעְבֵּץ: "אִם בָּרֵךְ תְּבָרֲכֵנִי וְהִרְבִּיתָ אֶת גְּבוּלִי" (דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים א ד, י) – הַגְּבוּל שֶׁלִּי תִּשְׁמוֹר שֶׁלֹּא לָצֵאת חוּץ מִגְּבוּל.
records.originEnglish: When a person prays for a spiritual virtue, he should pray that it not exceed his capacity, as it is written: "Remove far from me vanity and lies" (Proverbs 30:8). Meaning, "vanity" (shav) denotes delusions of chaos, and "word" (davar) denotes words of Torah as noted above in Section 183 from Ta'anit 10b; and even words of Torah, if they are beyond his vessel so that they will prove false and cease—remove them far from me. And he concluded upon this: "Give me neither poverty nor riches... lest I be full and deny, etc." (ibid. 30:8–9), for if he ascends to spiritual rungs that do not match the capacity of his receptive vessel, he will arrive at pride and falsehood, Heaven forbid. And concerning this Ya'betz prayed: "Oh that You would bless me indeed, and enlarge my border" (I Chronicles 4:10)—guard my boundary that I not spill beyond my proper border.
records.targetHebrew: ועל כן כשחזר ממצרים נאמר: "ואברם כבד מאד", היינו אחר שנתברר בעניות בבירור גמור בנסיון הראשון, נאמר "כבד מאד" לשון כבידות, שהיה ירא לנפשו מפני העשירות, כתפלת שלמה המלך עליו השלום (משלי ל, ח): "ראש ועשר אל תתן לי". ובלוט לא נאמר לשון "כבד", רק נאמר: "וגם ללוט ההלך את אברם היה וכולי", ואין "ויהי" אלא לשון שמחה כי לא היתה בו שום יראה כלל; מה שאין כן באברהם כתיב "כבד" מפני היראה, על כן כתיב: "וילך למסעיו... ויקרא שם אברם וכולי", כי גם עתה היה מתיירא מהעשירות כנ"ל, וכן בירר בכל ענינים.
records.targetEnglish: When he returned from Egypt it therefore says, ‘Avram was very heavy.’ After he had been completely clarified in poverty through the first trial, ‘very heavy’ expresses a burden: he feared for himself because of wealth, like Shlomo's prayer, ‘Give me neither poverty nor wealth.’ Of Lot it does not say ‘heavy,’ only that Lot who went with Avram also possessed property. The expression indicates gladness, for he had no fear at all. Of Avraham, by contrast, it says ‘heavy’ because of his fear. Hence, ‘He went on his journeys … and Avram called there’: even now he was concerned about wealth. In this way he clarified himself in every circumstance.
records.translationProvenance: Akiva Publishing original English translation, checked against the complete cited Hebrew paragraph during the comprehensive Tzidkat HaTzadik review; source quotation is separate from the editorial explanation.

records.themeTitle: Manna as light made into nourishment
records.themeSummary: The nourishment image includes a form in which divine illumination can be received by the creature.
records.explanation: Kometz HaMinchah explains why the Zohar describes powers of limitation as grinding manna.
